# Execise 1

Estimating the simple linear regressions

$$Y_{i,1} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + u_i$$ and $$Y_{i,2} = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 X_i + v_i$$.

We define $Q_i = X_i - 10$.

## Proof that $\widehat{\delta_1} = \widehat{\beta_1}$

We estimate $$Y_{i,1} = \delta_0 + \delta_1 Q_i + u_i$$

We have $$Q_i = X_i - 10 \quad \Rightarrow \quad X_i = Q_i + 10.$$

Substituting into the original regression gives $$Y_{i,1} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + u_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1(Q_i + 10) + u_i.$$

Rearranging: $$Y_{i,1} = (\beta_0 + 10\beta_1) + \beta_1 Q_i + u_i.$$

Comparing this to $$Y_{i,1} = \delta_0 + \delta_1 Q_i + u_i,$$ we obtain $$\delta_0 = \beta_0 + 10\beta_1 \quad \text{and} \quad \delta_1 = \beta_1.$$

Hence, $$\widehat{\delta_1} = \widehat{\beta_1}.$$

Conclusion: adding or subtracting a constant from a regressor does not affect the OLS slope coefficient. It only changes the intercept. In this case, $$\widehat{\delta_0} = \widehat{\beta_0} + 10\widehat{\beta_1}.$$
